Discover what hangs off the target before mutation. Persist full content and relations,
including every batch member and pagination page. Save pre/post location mappings for moves.
Record identity changes and inaccessible content as recovery limitations.
skill:
Large MCP output saved to a tool-results file is captured data, not failure. Read that local file with Python, extract/decode its payload, and copy the verified archive to the action directory; do not re-run the export or paste base64 into the prompt.

ARCHIVE PORTABILITY: BusyBox tar does not support GNU --null/--files-from. For known target directories use tar -czf - -C <parent> <relative-paths> | base64, with shell pipefail enabled where supported. Prefer archiving the resolved directory over an unsupported filename pipeline. For individual files use base64 <path>. Capture command errors; empty output is failure. Decode whitespace-normalized base64 and open the tar archive locally, verify expected paths/counts/hashes before reporting capture; never treat a successful final pipeline command as proof.

POLICY AND CASCADING DATA: Before patch/apply of configuration that controls retention, TTL, cleanup, pruning or storage, capture the dependent data the new policy can delete, not only the configuration object. Inspect namespace workload manifests for consumers of the named ConfigMap/Secret (volumes, envFrom/env and command arguments), follow their PVC mounts, and capture the affected existing bytes before returning. Restoring an old policy cannot recreate data already deleted by its controller. If consumers or affected bytes cannot be identified/captured, report the gap explicitly rather than declaring the config-only backup sufficient.

BOUND PVC CAPTURE: A bound volume may contain data even when no pod mounts it. Enumerate all pods in the namespace and match spec.volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName; never assume app=<claim name>. If no usable mount exists, create a dedicated temporary read-only Pod via kubectl_apply using the exact claim, wait until Ready, then exec_in_pod to inventory paths and SHA256 and tar/base64 the files. Save PVC/PV manifests and decoded archive outside the cluster in this action directory. Use python3 base64.b64decode(payload,validate=True), tarfile r:gz and verify file counts and hashes; keep archive base64 output separate from hash lines. Delete only your temporary helper after verified durable files exist. Lack of mounted pods is not evidence of empty data. RBAC, scheduling, invalid/truncated output or unavailable tools mean capture failed, never YAML-only success.

Backup guidance for Kubernetes MCP operations. Use the triggering call's actual cluster alias and namespace. Resolve every selector and manifest document, follow pagination, expand owner/dependent resources, and save actual data outside the cluster before mutation. Prefer full YAML: some JSON list responses contain only names/status. Preserve the original manifest, plus a separate restore copy without status, uid, resourceVersion, generation, creationTimestamp and managedFields; handle last-applied/revision annotations deliberately. A manifest is not a data-volume backup. Bound PVCs require their actual mounted bytes, PV/claim mappings and checksums; restoring only YAML or a Pending claim is insufficient. Recreated UIDs/IPs, process memory and history may not be recoverable.

[1] Delete: resolve all names/labels/documents; save full target YAML and cascading ownerReferences dependents. Include workload revisions/pods, namespace resources, and Service addresses/endpoints. Secret data may be redacted: capture individual .data keys via kubectl_generic jsonpath when permitted. PVC/PV deletion additionally requires mounted data bytes and hashes. Restore data and dependency-ordered sanitized objects; record identity/address changes.
[2] Apply: enumerate every YAML document. Existing object: save complete pre-state, including keys an apply may prune, and workload/revision/volume dependents. Absent object: record absence and identify what this call creates. Recovery restores prior objects and deletes only confirmed additions. Pass manifest content inline when the server cannot read host files.
[3] Create: record prior existence/absence and full manifests of existing targets. Inspect every member even on error because a multi-object create can partially succeed. Pin newly created kind/name/namespace/UID and recover by deleting only those creations, including dependent data where applicable; never use cleanup as a universal inverse.
[4] Patch: save complete target YAML/JSON, not just patched keys. Merge patches may delete fields, reorder lists or introduce keys. Keep an unmodified capture and a sanitized restore copy; restore exact prior values and remove newly introduced keys. Verify target and affected children, not merely a successful apply return.
[5] Scale: save full workload and explicit replicas, full pod manifests and any matching HPA. Include unmanaged/pod-local/emptyDir data before pod loss. Recover desired replicas and HPA state and verify readiness. Recreated pod identity, logs and memory are not preserved by replica count alone.
[6] Rollout undo/restart/pause/resume: save workload spec/template/paused/replicas, revision number, all matching ReplicaSets or ControllerRevisions and pod state/data. Recover from the captured template/revision and prior paused state; verify readiness. Do not assume undo can recover a revision already removed by history retention.
[7] Cordon/uncordon: save whether spec.unschedulable was absent or false, all taints and node labels/annotations; inventory node-bound pods and owners. Restore exact prior field presence and values. Any evicted bare pod or local data needs its own manifest/bytes, not just uncordon.
[8] Bare pod delete: capture full YAML, logs and container/emptyDir data before deletion; no owner will recreate a bare pod. Restore sanitized manifest inline, repopulate data and verify bytes. Pod UID/IP/times, emptyDir and process memory do not return from YAML alone.
[9] Start port-forward: persist resourceType, resourceName, namespace, localPort and targetPort at creation. Pin the version-specific derived id '<resourceType>-<resourceName>-<localPort>'. Recovery stops only that forward. Existing tunnel/socket state is outside this creation-only inverse.
[10] Drain: dryRun first to resolve the actual eviction set. Save node scheduling/taints plus every affected pod's manifest, owners, logs and local/volume bytes, including workloads outside the default namespace. Restore node state, recreate bare pods and data; verify. Dry-run evidence does not establish successful live drain recovery.
[11] exec_in_pod writes: enumerate every affected path. Export actual bytes using base64 plus wc/sha256sum; persist, decode and compare the artifact hash before mutation. Restore those bytes and verify independently. Record ownership/mode needs separately; content-only tests do not prove metadata or process-state recovery.
[12] kubectl_generic mutation: label/annotate requires full YAML plus original values AND absent-key flags. Recover existing values with --overwrite; remove originally absent keys with key-. For other mutation verbs apply the relevant resource/data capture, rather than treating the generic tool as a read.
[13] Set context: save the exact current context, detailed contexts and raw kubeconfig; preserve missing namespace versus explicit default. Restore the original pointer/config and verify. This changes the MCP server's global target, not just this caller; get/list are reads.
[14] Stop port-forward: there is no exposed active-forward enumeration on this server. Recover the five creation fields from prior creation records before stopping; an id alone is insufficient. Recreate with the same fields and verify listening; existing TCP sessions cannot be restored.
[15] Cleanup: on the tested 4.1.4 build the manager never registers created resources, so cleanup reports success but deletes none. Explicitly delete pinned creations; do not use cleanup to reverse create/apply. This is a version-specific no-op observation, not a general guarantee for other builds.

Archive integrity: never manually retype a long base64 response with Write. Extract the exact original tool-result text programmatically from its saved output/session file, decode it, run gzip -t (not only tar listing), and verify every file against the captured SHA256 inventory. A parseable tar or matching byte count alone is insufficient. If exact bytes cannot be persisted and verified, report capture failure.

patterns.skill:
BEFORE any kubectl_delete, resolve the full target set into concrete named objects - re-run kubectl_get with the SAME namespace/labelSelector/fieldSelector/allNamespaces (or parse the manifest) and never assume one object; if the list response carries metadata.continue, follow every page. For each resolved object persist the COMPLETE live manifest via kubectl_get output=yaml into a file OUTSIDE the cluster (a name/URL listing or a model-context table is not a backup). SECRETS ARE SPECIAL: kubectl_get redacts data to '***' - capture them with kubectl_generic {command:'get', resourceType:'secret', name, namespace, args:['-o','jsonpath={.data.<key>}']} per key, and record explicitly if RBAC denies read. Then expand dependants that cascade: for a Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet also dump its ReplicaSets/ControllerRevisions, pods and kubectl_rollout history; for a Namespace run list_api_resources namespaced=true and kubectl_generic get <all types> in that namespace, noting which objects are controller-recreated (kube-root-ca.crt, default ServiceAccount) versus real user data; for a PVC dump the bound PV and its claimRef; for a Service dump spec.clusterIP (it is NOT preserved on recreate) plus Endpoints/EndpointSlices; for any owner dump all children whose ownerReferences point at its uid; for ConfigMaps/Secrets dump the workloads referencing them. Validate each artifact before allowing the delete: it must be non-empty, parse as YAML, contain the same COUNT as the live list, and match per-object content checksums - and when re-serializing, force string quoting so values like '08'/'09'/'true' are not retyped into ints/bools. To RESTORE, re-apply with kubectl_apply passing the saved YAML INLINE via the manifest parameter (filename reads the MCP server's filesystem, not yours), stripping resourceVersion, uid, creationTimestamp, generation, status, managedFields and deployment.kubernetes.io/revision, and STAGE the applies: cluster-scoped objects (Namespaces, CRDs, PVs, ClusterRoles) in their own call, then namespaced RBAC, PVCs, ConfigMaps/Secrets, then workloads - a single manifest mixing cluster-scoped and namespaced docs is rejected and applies only partially. Record as LIMITATIONS that recreated objects get new UIDs/resourceVersions, that pods return with new names/IPs and their logs and ephemeral state are gone, that rollout history resets to one revision, that Service clusterIP changes unless re-specified, that PV-backed volume data is not recovered by re-apply, that unreadable/redacted Secrets could not be captured, and that force/gracePeriodSeconds=0 deletes may orphan external cloud resources.

BOUND PVC DATA CAPTURE:
Before deleting a PVC, resolve every concrete named claim selected by the original namespace/name/selector and read its bound PV, claimRef, reclaim policy and volume mode. Save these manifests outside the cluster. A Pending claim is not a verified Bound-volume capture. For every Bound filesystem claim, enumerate its current mounting pods. Use an existing usable mount, or create one dedicated temporary Pod via kubectl_apply with this exact claim and a read-only mount; poll kubectl_get until Ready. Never delete or alter unrelated pods to attach a volume. With exec_in_pod, inventory files and hashes, then tar the mounted files and base64 the archive to tool output. Decode on the agent and write archive plus inventory and checksums into THIS action directory; verify archive is nonempty, decodes, contains all intended files and matches source hashes. This local verification is required capture work. Delete only the temporary helper Pod you created. Record failures for RBAC, scheduling, block volumes, inconsistent live writes, truncation or unsupported volume mode instead of claiming metadata suffices. Restore uses saved PV/claim mapping and claim manifests plus actual saved archive bytes in the restored mount, then rechecks file hashes. Never call a YAML-only restore complete. The procedure is derived from the existing successful Opus read-only mount -> exec tar/base64 -> local extraction/hash evidence; this new route itself still requires an independent live regression. LOCAL SAVE REQUIREMENTS: Use python3 (do not assume node exists). Save PVC and PV tool responses verbatim, including labels, annotations and all spec fields; do not hand-reconstruct reduced manifests or UIDs. Request archive-only base64 output separately from file hash inventory, or delimit it with exact ARCHIVE_BEGIN and ARCHIVE_END lines. Never decode a concatenation of hash lines and base64. Strictly decode only the framed payload using base64.b64decode(payload, validate=True), open with tarfile mode r:gz, and verify every expected regular-file path/count and SHA256 before reporting success. Write required metadata JSON using Python json.dump. Use checked subprocess return codes; do not chain fallible commands with semicolons. A missing file, invalid archive or failed comparison means backup_failed; preserve raw output and do not claim success. Only remove your helper after verified durable archive and manifests exist.
patterns.verify_note: Executed the full capture -> unchanged kubectl_delete -> restore -> independent re-read cycle five times (labelSelector batch of 12, Deployment with RS/Pod/Endpoints cascade, Secret, Namespace cascade, manifest-mode). All destructions were confirmed by re-read before restoring, and all restores were verified by independent jsonpath re-reads comparing data, labels, spec fields and UIDs rather than by the apply output. The proposed pattern was broadly correct but wrong in three concrete ways that I corrected: (1) kubectl_get output=yaml redacts Secret data as '***', so it is NOT a valid backup for Secrets - kubectl_generic -o jsonpath={.data.<key>} is required and is now in capture_tools; (2) kubectl_apply's filename parameter reads the MCP server's filesystem, not the agent's, so restores must inline the saved YAML via the manifest parameter; (3) kubectl_apply forces a namespace flag, so a manifest mixing a cluster-scoped Namespace with namespaced objects fails AND applies partially - restore must be staged scope-by-scope. Outcome is partial, not full: spec/data recovery was byte-identical everywhere, but UIDs, pod identities, rollout history and Service clusterIP were observably lost.

patterns.action: Apply a manifest (server-side upsert that can overwrite an existing object)
patterns.skill: Before any kubectl_apply, parse the manifest (or the file named in the call) and enumerate EVERY document in it — a multi-doc YAML is a batch and each member needs its own backup, so iterate all of them and never stop at the first. For each kind/name/namespace, first run kubectl_get with output=yaml (a kubectl_generic `get k1,k2 --selector=...` or per-object get both work; jsonpath range-over-map fails, use `--output=go-template=...` if you need a compact signature). Branch on existence: (a) object EXISTS -> persist its full pre-state manifest to a durable file outside the cluster (e.g. /work/artifacts/prestate-<kind>-<name>.yaml) — this manifest IS the restore artifact; strip status, resourceVersion, uid and creationTimestamp only if you also record them separately, and keep every data key (ConfigMaps/Secrets can hold dozens of keys that a shorter apply will silently prune via kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration, so an incomplete capture loses them permanently); (b) object does NOT exist (kubectl_get returns {"error":"Resource ... not found"}) -> record it in a created-by-this-action list so restore DELETES it. Also capture the dependants the apply will disturb: for workloads the current deployment.kubernetes.io/revision, metadata.generation, `rollout history`, the active ReplicaSet name and the current pod names/replica counts; for Services the allocated clusterIP/nodePorts; for volume changes the bound PVC/PV. Verify each artifact is non-empty and parseable AND prove it equals the source BEFORE the action — compare key counts plus a content checksum (sha256 of a go-template key=value dump), because counts alone do not prove fidelity. If dryRun=true, the apply mutates nothing (verified: resourceVersion unchanged) so no backup is needed. On RESTORE: kubectl_apply the saved pre-state manifests (pass them via `manifest:` — this MCP transport rejects `filename:` server-side paths; add force=true only if a conflict blocks the apply), then kubectl_delete each object recorded as created-by-this-action, then kubectl_delete the residue ReplicaSet the clobbered rollout left behind so rollout history and the RS set match the pre-state. Finally re-read and compare independently: data checksum, labels, annotations, spec fields, uid/creationTimestamp, and dependant state (ReplicaSet name, ready replica count). LIMITATIONS to report rather than hide: restored objects keep new resourceVersions and generations; the rollout revision counter only moves forward so the original revision number and its history entry are gone; pods are recreated with new names/UIDs/IPs and their ephemeral state, plus already-pulled/already-run images, are not reversible.

patterns.skill: kubectl_create only ADDS objects - it was observed to NEVER modify a pre-existing object (AlreadyExists error, uid/resourceVersion unchanged), so the reversal is a pinned delete, not an apply-back. BEFORE it runs: enumerate every document in the manifest (resourceType/name/namespace, and note any generateName), and for the subcommand form the single resourceType/name/namespace; kubectl_get output=yaml each one and persist the result to a durable file outside the cluster, verifying each artifact is non-empty - objects that already exist get a full prior-manifest artifact (diff baseline / accidental-delete insurance), the rest are marked candidate-new. AFTER it runs, ALWAYS re-read the namespace even if the tool returned an error: kubectl_create is NOT atomic - an AlreadyExists on one document still creates every other document, and on the error path the tool returns no output at all, so generated names and successfully created objects are only discoverable by kubectl_get (use labelSelector or name listing, never recency). Record the confirmed newly-created set as kind+namespace+name. On RESTORE: kubectl_delete each recorded newly-created object pinned by kind+namespace+name (never by recency, never with labelSelector alone if pre-existing objects share the label); controller objects (Deployment/Job/StatefulSet) reclaim their cascading children automatically - verify with kubectl_get all. patterns.skill: BEFORE scaling, capture the pre-state to a durable file OUTSIDE the cluster: (1) kubectl_get with output:'yaml' on the target workload (resourceType/name/namespace) and persist BOTH spec.replicas and the full manifest; (2) kubectl_get resourceType:'pods' with the workload's labelSelector and output:'yaml' -- NOT output:'json', which returns only name/status/createdAt and silently drops uid, podIP and spec, so it is a listing and not a backup -- and record each pod's name, uid, podIP and node; (3) kubectl_get resourceType:'hpa' in the namespace and persist any HPA whose scaleTargetRef matches this workload, including minReplicas/maxReplicas, since it may re-scale the workload afterwards. VERIFY the captured replica value is present and non-null (a missing spec.replicas means the count defaults to 1 and the original is unrecoverable) and checksum the artifact before the scale runs. Note kubectl_scale also accepts resourceType statefulset/replicaset. On RESTORE, kubectl_patch patchType:'strategic' with patchData {"spec":{"replicas":<CAPTURED_REPLICAS>}} and re-read with kubectl_get output:'yaml' to confirm spec.replicas AND status.readyReplicas both equal the captured number. LIMITATIONS to state plainly: this restores the COUNT only. Pods terminated by a scale-down never come back -- replacements have new names, UIDs and IPs, and their logs and ephemeral local state are gone (StatefulSet pods regain their ordinal NAMES but still get new UIDs/IPs). metadata.generation and resourceVersion stay advanced. If an HPA owns the replica count the restored value may be immediately overridden, so restore/confirm the HPA bounds too. If the StatefulSet sets persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy.whenScaled=Delete, scaling down destroys PVC data that no replica-count restore can recover.

patterns.skill: BEFORE any mutating rollout subcommand (undo/restart/pause/resume), persist to a file OUTSIDE the cluster: (a) kubectl_get({resourceType:'deployment|statefulset|daemonset', name, namespace, output:'yaml'}) - the full manifest including metadata.annotations['deployment.kubernetes.io/revision'], .spec.paused, .spec.replicas and the complete .spec.template; (b) the full revision history for its selector - kubectl_get({resourceType:'replicasets'|'controllerrevisions', namespace, labelSelector:<deployment selector>, output:'yaml'}) for EVERY page - recording for each entry the name, uid, pod-template-hash, the deployment.kubernetes.io/revision (or ControllerRevision .revision) number AND its pod template; (c) kubectl_get pods -o wide for the current pod names/IPs (for post-hoc diffing only - pods are NOT restorable). Pin the target as the pair (revision number, ReplicaSet/ControllerRevision name), because revision numbers are renumbered by every undo. Verify the artifact files are non-empty and that the RS/CR count matches the live count before acting. ON RESTORE: re-resolve the captured ReplicaSet/ControllerRevision NAME to its CURRENT revision number via kubectl_get, then kubectl_rollout({subCommand:'undo', resourceType, name, namespace, revision:<that number>}) - pass it as 'revision'; 'toRevision' is ignored by this MCP tool and silently degrades to a plain undo. This single call reverses undo AND restart (it clears the injected kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt annotation). For pause/resume, restore from the CAPTURED .spec.paused value: if it was true re-run subCommand:'pause', if it was absent/false run subCommand:'resume' (resume errors with 'is not paused' if it was never paused). If the target revision was pruned from history, fall back to kubectl_apply({manifest:<saved manifest>}) to recreate the prior pod template - but note apply alone will NOT remove a restartedAt annotation. Finally re-read with kubectl_get -o yaml and diff .spec against the artifact, and confirm kubectl_rollout subCommand:'status'. LIMITATIONS: 'status' and 'history' are read-only and need no backup; the restored state lands on a NEW, higher revision number and generation; pods are replaced with new names/UIDs/IPs and their logs and ephemeral state are unrecoverable; revisions pruned by revisionHistoryLimit are gone.

patterns.skill: A drain is a mass pod-eviction plus a cordon; treat it as 'delete every pod on this node' and back up accordingly. FIRST run the SAME call with dryRun:true - it mutates nothing and prints the exact list of pods that would be evicted, which is your resolved target set (no other tool scopes a drain; node_management has no namespace filter, so on a single-node cluster the target set is the whole cluster including kube-system). Persist to a file OUTSIDE the cluster: (a) kubectl_get({resourceType:'nodes',name:<NODE>,output:'yaml'}) recording whether spec.unschedulable is ABSENT versus explicitly false and the COMPLETE spec.taints list - restore must reproduce absence, not write false; (b) the pod inventory with owners, kubectl_generic({command:'get',resourceType:'pods',allNamespaces:true,args:['--field-selector','spec.nodeName=<NODE>','-o','custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,OWNER:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind,OWNERNAME:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name,PHASE:.status.phase,UID:.metadata.uid']}). Read that inventory before deciding anything: pods with an OWNER are recreated by their controller and need no manifest backup, but pods with EMPTY ownerReferences are bare - drain REFUSES them unless force:true, and with force:true they are deleted with nothing to recreate them, so their full manifests (and logs, and any container-local data) are the only restore source. Also save out-of-cluster any state that was written INTO a container after start (exec-written files, emptyDir contents): eviction destroys it and no controller regenerates it unless the pod spec itself does. Never claim a drain was exercised by deleting pods yourself - run the tool. drain is a no-op without confirmDrain:true; that refusal is a guard, not a failure.

mcp__k8s__kubectl_generic({command:'get', resourceType:'pods', allNamespaces:true, args:['--field-selector','spec.nodeName=<NODE>','-o','custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,OWNER:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind,OWNERNAME:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name,PHASE:.status.phase,UID:.metadata.uid']})   # resolved pod inventory + owners -> file

# for every pod whose OWNER column is <none>: mcp__k8s__kubectl_get({resourceType:'pods',name:'<POD>',namespace:'<NS>',output:'yaml'}) -> file  (see pattern 'Delete a bare/unmanaged pod')

patterns.action: Execute a command inside a pod that durably modifies a file in the container (exec_in_pod)
patterns.skill: Treat any non-read exec as a durable mutation of container-local state. BEFORE executing, parse the command array for every path it writes, and for each one transport the ACTUAL BYTES out of the cluster - not a listing, not a path, not a summary in context: exec_in_pod(['sh','-c','base64 <PATH>']) and write the returned text to a host file, plus ['sh','-c','wc -c <PATH>; sha256sum <PATH>'] so you can prove artifact==source BEFORE you destroy anything. Decode the base64 locally and check its sha256 equals the in-pod sha256; if they differ, abort rather than mutate. Restore by feeding the artifact back the same way: exec_in_pod(['sh','-c','printf %s <BASE64_FROM_FILE> | base64 -d > <PATH>; sha256sum <PATH>; wc -c <PATH>']), then re-read independently and compare the base64 to the artifact. Note exec_in_pod does NOT interpret shell syntax - redirects and pipes only work because the command array explicitly starts with ['sh','-c',...]; a bare argv cannot redirect. This recovers CONTENT only, and only while the container is still running: the container filesystem is ephemeral, so if the pod restarts or is evicted (see the drain pattern) the file is gone regardless, and mode/owner/mtime are not covered.

# locally: base64 -d <ARTIFACT>.b64 > <ARTIFACT> ; sha256sum <ARTIFACT>   -> MUST equal the in-pod digest before proceeding
# ... original action: mcp__k8s__exec_in_pod({name:'<POD>', namespace:'<NS>', command:[...writing command...]}) ...

patterns.action: Change a label or annotation with kubectl_generic (command 'label' / 'annotate', --overwrite)
patterns.skill: kubectl_generic is a pass-through verb runner with no undo and no server-side history, so the ONLY thing that makes a mutating call reversible is a capture taken before it. For the label/annotate verbs: capture the full live manifest with kubectl_get(output:'yaml') to a host file AND pin the individual values with a jsonpath read (kubectl_generic command:'get', args:['-o','jsonpath={.metadata.labels}{.metadata.annotations.<KEY>}']) so the restore reads a value out of a file rather than out of context. Note the direction matters: overwriting an EXISTING key is reversed with the same verb plus --overwrite and the captured value, but a key that did NOT exist before must be reversed with the 'key-' removal form instead - so the capture has to record absence, not just values. When you diff afterwards, ignore metadata.resourceVersion, metadata.generation and status.observedGeneration: they are monotonic server counters and can never be restored. Do NOT generalise this to other kubectl_generic verbs; delete/replace/edit/set/taint each destroy different things and need their own pattern.

patterns.action: Switch the active kubectl context (kubectl_context operation='set')
patterns.skill: Only operation='set' mutates; list and get are reads. The mutation is durable and GLOBAL to the MCP server process - it rewrites current-context in the server host's kubeconfig file, so it changes the default target of every later call by every caller, not just yours. BEFORE the set: kubectl_context(operation:'get',showCurrent:true) to pin the exact current context name, kubectl_context(operation:'list',detailed:true) for the full list, AND kubectl_generic(command:'config',subCommand:'view',args:['-o','json']) for the RAW kubeconfig - you need the raw view because kubectl_context list REPORTS namespace 'default' for a context whose kubeconfig entry has NO namespace field, and round-tripping that display value would silently change behaviour. Abort if the captured name is empty or a placeholder; with no valid pre-state there is no way back. Restore is kubectl_context(operation:'set') with the captured name, then re-read and additionally diff the raw kubeconfig. Remember the pointer is all you get back: anything you created while the wrong context was current still lives in the other context and must be reverted separately.

patterns.action: Stop an existing port-forward (stop_port_forward) - rebuilding it needs creation args captured at START time
patterns.skill: There is NO tool on this server that enumerates active forwards - tools/list exposes only port_forward and stop_port_forward. That is the whole problem: once a forward is stopped, the server can tell you nothing about what it was, so the five rebuild fields (resourceType, resourceName, namespace, localPort, targetPort) MUST be written to a host file at CREATION time, not at stop time. port_forward also returns no id at all; the registry id is the derived, undocumented string '<resourceType>-<resourceName>-<localPort>' - record the five fields, not just the id, because the format is a server-version detail. To restore, call port_forward again with the captured fields; the re-created forward binds the same local port and answers to the same derived id. What CANNOT be restored is traffic: stop_port_forward kills the forwarding process, so established TCP sessions and any in-flight request are dropped and cannot be replayed - quiesce clients first and treat the tunnel as a fresh one afterwards. Note also that a port_forward which fails because the local port is already bound leaves NO registry entry, so a start failure needs no teardown. See the companion pattern 'Start a port-forward' for the opposite direction.

patterns.skill: Do NOT use cleanup as the inverse of kubectl_create/kubectl_apply. On the installed build here (mcp-server-kubernetes 4.1.4) cleanup() aborts tracked watches and then deletes only the entries in the manager's in-memory this.resources list - and that list is populated ONLY by trackResource(), which has NO CALLERS anywhere in the installed dist. So nothing you create through the exposed kubectl tools is ever registered, and cleanup returns {"success":true} having deleted nothing. An agent that relies on it to tidy up will silently leak every object it made. Track your own objects and tear them down with explicit kubectl_delete calls against names you recorded. Before trusting this on ANY other server, re-read the installed source: the behaviour is a property of this dist, not of the tool's contract - the tool takes no arguments, is flagged destructiveHint, exposes no dryRun and no way to enumerate its tracked set, so a build that does wire up trackResource would become destructive with an identical call signature. Even then it would be only a partial teardown: deleteResource's switch handles ONLY pod, deployment, service and cronjob, silently skipping every other kind, and the tracked list is process memory that a restart empties. cleanup does not touch port-forwards - stop those with stop_port_forward.

limitations: VERSION-SPECIFIC BEHAVIOR, NOT A CONTRACT. The no-op is a consequence of trackResource having no callers in this dist. If a future build wires trackResource into the create/apply handlers, the same argument-less call becomes destructive with no change to its signature or its description. Re-verify against the installed source before trusting it on any other server.
The tool still takes NO arguments: inputSchema is {} - no namespace, selector, resourceType, dryRun or confirm - and carries annotations.destructiveHint: true. A caller cannot scope or preview it.

The tracked set is unreadable through the protocol: no listing tool, resources/list returns only 5 static URI templates, prompts/list has one unrelated prompt. Even on a build where tracking works, you could not enumerate what cleanup is about to delete before calling it.

The tracked set is process memory only - not persisted, emptied by a server restart - so even a build that tracked correctly would forget objects across restarts, making cleanup an unreliable teardown by construction.

deleteResource handles only pod, deployment, service and cronjob. On any build, a tracked namespace, configmap, secret, statefulset, daemonset, pvc or job would be silently skipped, so cleanup is at best a PARTIAL teardown even when tracking works.
cleanup does not touch port-forwards; those are stopped only via stop_port_forward (see the stop_port_forward pattern).

exclusions.action: Relying on exec_in_pod restore across a pod restart
exclusions.reason: A container's writable layer is ephemeral. Verified in item 1: the drain destroyed the pod and its replacement's file matched the original digest ONLY because the container's own command regenerates it. Exec-written state that is not in a volume and not reproducible from the pod spec is lost on any restart, eviction, scale or drain, regardless of backup.

exclusions.action: Recovering pod identity after any eviction/recreation (drain, scale, rollout, delete)
exclusions.reason: Pod names, uids, podIPs, container restart state and pod logs do not survive. Confirmed again in item 1 (all 8 pods got new names and uids after the drain). Recipes recover AVAILABILITY and the owning controller's identity, never pod identity.

exclusions.action: Recovering client connections in flight through a port-forward when it is stopped
exclusions.reason: stop_port_forward kills the forwarding process; established TCP sessions and in-progress requests are dropped and cannot be replayed. The definition can be rebuilt, the traffic cannot.

Any future claim of tested HTTP forwarding must come from new evidence.
